# `filter()`: rows by condition {.section-break}

`slice()` picks rows by position. `filter()` picks them by what's in them.

## Keep the rows where a condition is true

Only the rows that pass the test are kept. All the columns stay.

::: small
`==` equals · `!=` does not equal · `<` `>` less, greater than · `<=` `>=` or equal to
:::

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(sex == 'female')
```

::: notes
Two equals signs to compare. The text value is in quotes. Comparisons: == != < > <= >=, the same ones as week 1.
:::

## The same with a number

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(age == 50)
```

::: notes
The number isn't in quotes.
:::

## `filter()` on one column {.try-it}

Keep only the passengers who boarded at Queenstown: the rows where `embarked` is equal to `Q`

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(___)
```

::: notes
filter(embarked == 'Q'): 123 rows. Q needs quotes. Run the starter as it is first if you like: object '___' not found is the error they'll see for a name R doesn't know.
:::

## `filter()` on one column {.try-it}

Keep only the rows where `fare` is greater than 5

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(___)
```

::: notes
filter(fare > 5): 1,288 rows.
:::

## Combining conditions: and

`&` means **and**: both must be true

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(age > 50 & sex == 'female')
```

::: notes
32 women over 50. A comma inside filter() means the same as &.
:::

## Combining conditions: or

`|` means **or**: either can be true

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(fare > 50 | pclass == 1)
```

::: notes
354 rows.
:::

## Two conditions at once {.try-it}

Keep only the passengers from first class who are also over 70

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(___ & ___)
```

::: small
Hint: `pclass` is a number, so no quotes. Write each condition in full: `age > 70`
:::

::: notes
filter(pclass == 1 & age > 70): 4 passengers. Artagaveytia (71), Barkworth (80), Cavendish (76), Goldschmidt (71).
:::

## A list of values: `%in%`

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(embarked %in% c('C', 'Q'))
```

A range of numbers works too: `age %in% 20:30`

::: notes
393 rows for C or Q. Try filter(age %in% 20:30).
:::

## Not: `!`

`!` flips a condition:

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(!embarked %in% c('C', 'Q'))
```

::: small
Optional: filter on text patterns with `str_detect()` in chapter 15. Not needed for the rest of the course.
:::

::: notes
916 rows: all of Southampton plus the 2 passengers with no port, because NA isn't in the list.
:::

## Spot the mistake

::: predict
**Predict** what happens with each, then run it.
:::

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(sex = 'female')
```

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(sex == female)
```

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(sex == 'Female')
```

. . .

::: small
Before you trust a filter, check the number of rows it returns. Does it make sense? Not sure how a value is spelled? Look with `count()` or `distinct()`.
:::

::: notes
1. One = sets an argument: an error that suggests ==.
2. No quotes: object 'female' not found.
3. No error, but 0 rows: R is case-sensitive. The quietest mistake is the worst one. Always check how many rows you got back.
:::

## Predict first, then run it {.try-it}

Which returns more rows, and why?

a)  `filter(pclass == 1, sex == 'female')`
b)  `filter(pclass == 1 | sex == 'female')`

Predict, then run each one here:

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(pclass == 1, sex == 'female')
```

::: notes
The second: 645 rows against 144. A comma means and, so the first keeps only first-class women; | keeps everyone in first class plus all women. These are in the style of the exam. Students can edit the cell to run b.
:::

## Predict first, then run it {.try-it}

Passengers younger than 10 **or** older than 60. Which is correct?

a)  `filter(age < 10, age > 60)`
b)  `filter(age < 10 | age > 60)`
c)  `filter(age %in% c(10, 60))`

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  filter(___)
```

::: notes
b, 115 rows. a asks for under 10 and over 60 at once: 0 rows, no error. c keeps only those aged exactly 10 or 60: 11 rows.
:::

# `mutate()`: new columns {.section-break}

Calculate something new from the columns you already have

## What would a Titanic ticket cost today?

£1 in 1910 is worth about £78.17 today (National Archives currency converter). A new column is added at the end. All the rows stay.

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  mutate(price_today = fare * 78.17) |>
  select(name, fare, price_today)
```

::: notes
The new column goes at the end; select() just brings it into view.
:::

## Functions inside `mutate()`

Functions work inside `mutate()` too:

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  mutate(age_in_years = round(age)) |>
  select(name, age, age_in_years)
```

::: notes
Nothing is saved unless you use <-.
:::

## New columns with `mutate()` {.try-it}

The ages were recorded five years too low. Make a new column, `corrected_age`, with the right value

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  mutate(corrected_age = ___)
```

::: notes
mutate(corrected_age = age + 5). Add |> select(name, age, corrected_age) to see it.
:::

## New columns with `mutate()` {.try-it}

Work out roughly the year each passenger was born. The Titanic sank in 1912

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  mutate(birth_year = ___)
```

::: notes
mutate(birth_year = 1912 - age), or round(1912 - age). Elisabeth Allen, 29, born about 1883.
:::

## The most expensive ticket {.try-it}

Who paid the highest fare, and what was it in today's money? Show only the name and the price today

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  ___ |>
  ___ |>
  ___
```

::: notes
mutate(price_today = fare * 78.17) |> slice_max(order_by = price_today, n = 1) |> select(name, price_today). arrange(-price_today) also works.
Four rows tie at £512.33, about £40,049: Mr and Mrs Cardeza, Gustave Lesurer and Anna Ward. They shared one ticket: the fare is per ticket, not per person. The shared-ticket problem from Thursday again.
:::

## New categories: `if_else()`

`if_else(test, value if true, value if false)`

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  mutate(status = if_else(age < 18, 'child', 'adult')) |>
  count(status)
```

. . .

::: predict
Passengers with no age get no status at all. Who are they, and does leaving them out change your story?
:::

::: notes
892 adults, 154 children, 263 NA. Passengers with no age get no status. Who are they, and does leaving them out change your story? count() is coming later today: it counts the rows for each value.
:::

## More than two: `case_when()`

`test ~ value`, checked in order: the first true one wins

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  mutate(status = case_when(
    age < 13 ~ 'child',
    age < 20 ~ 'teenager',
    age >= 20 ~ 'adult'
  )) |>
  count(status)
```

::: notes
Because they're checked in order, the second line doesn't need age >= 13 as well. Try adding a line: .default = 'unknown', to label the NAs.
:::

# `summarise()` and `group_by()` {.section-break}

Where data analysis really starts: counting things

## Many rows become one

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  summarise(passengers = n(),
            total_fare = sum(fare, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_fare = mean(fare, na.rm = TRUE))
```

. . .

::: predict
**Predict:** what happens without `na.rm = TRUE`?
:::

::: notes
1309 passengers, total 43,550, mean 33.3. Then delete na.rm = TRUE and run again: NA, because one fare is missing and R won't guess. tally() is a shortcut for summarise(n = n()).
:::

## Useful summary functions

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `n()` | count rows |
| `sum()` | add up |
| `mean()`, `median()` | the middle |
| `min()`, `max()` | the extremes |
| `n_distinct()` | count different values |

. . .

::: predict
**Why `na.rm = TRUE`?** One fare is missing (and 263 ages). Ask for the mean of a column with any NA in it and the answer is NA: R won't guess. `na.rm = TRUE` means "remove the NAs first".
:::

## `summarise()` the whole list {.try-it}

What is the average age of all the passengers? Use `mean()`

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  summarise(average_age = ___)
```

::: notes
summarise(average_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)): 29.9. Without na.rm: NA, as 263 ages are missing.
:::

## `summarise()` the whole list {.try-it}

What is the highest fare anyone paid? Use `max()`

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  summarise(max_fare = ___)
```

::: notes
summarise(max_fare = max(fare, na.rm = TRUE)): 512.33, the shared ticket from earlier.
:::

## `group_by()` on its own

On its own, `group_by()` changes nothing you can see:

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  group_by(sex)
```

::: notes
Point out Groups: sex [2] in the printout.
:::

## One summary per group

`group_by()` changes what the next verb does:

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(total = n())
```

::: small
**Split** into groups → **summarise** each → **combine** the results. Group by two columns, `group_by(sex, pclass)`, and you get one row for every combination: six groups.
:::

::: notes
Split, summarise each group, combine: female 466, male 843.
:::

## Group, then summarise {.try-it}

Make a summary with the average age of male and female passengers, in a column called `average_age`

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  group_by(___) |>
  summarise(average_age = ___)
```

::: small
Hint: which column makes the groups? And remember `na.rm = TRUE`
:::

::: notes
group_by(sex) |> summarise(average_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)): female 28.7, male 30.6.
:::

## Groups change other verbs too

The five oldest in **each** class:

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  group_by(pclass) |>
  slice_max(order_by = age, n = 5)
```

::: notes
15 rows: 5 per class.
:::

## Groups change other verbs too

A group total on every row:

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  group_by(pclass) |>
  mutate(total_class = n())
```

::: small
`ungroup()` removes the groups again. Unexpected results after a `group_by()`? A leftover group is often why.
:::

::: notes
With mutate, all 1,309 rows are kept, with a new column: everyone in first class gets 323.
:::

## Counting by group {.try-it}

Count the passengers by both `sex` and `pclass`

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  ___ |>
  ___
```

::: notes
group_by(sex, pclass) |> summarise(total = n()): female 144 / 106 / 216, male 179 / 171 / 493.
:::

## Counting by group {.try-it}

`embarked`: C = Cherbourg, Q = Queenstown, S = Southampton. How many passengers got on at each location? And what was the average fare at each?

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  ___ |>
  ___
```

::: notes
group_by(embarked) |> summarise(total = n(), avg_fare = mean(fare, na.rm = TRUE)): C 270 (62.3), Q 123 (12.4), S 914 (27.4), and 2 NA (80). Why is Cherbourg so high? More first-class passengers boarded there.
Shortcut: count(embarked) is group_by(embarked) |> summarise(n = n()).
:::

## Groups with `mutate()` {.try-it}

Add a column, `total_embarked`, that gives the number of passengers who boarded at the **same port** as that passenger. Every row stays

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  ___ |>
  mutate(total_embarked = ___)
```

::: small
Hint: like `total_class` a few slides back, but grouped by port
:::

::: notes
group_by(embarked) |> mutate(total_embarked = n()). Every row kept; everyone from Southampton gets 914, Cherbourg 270, Queenstown 123.
:::

## Groups with `slice_min()` {.try-it}

Who are the five youngest male and five youngest female passengers who boarded at each location?

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  group_by(___, ___) |>
  ___
```

::: notes
group_by(embarked, sex) |> slice_min(order_by = age, n = 5): 34 rows, not 30. slice_min() keeps ties (several babies aged 1), and the NA group only has 2 passengers. Point out the five Rice brothers, aged 2 to 10, who boarded at Queenstown: people behind the rows.
:::

## Back to "women and children first" {.try-it}

Calculate the survival rate for each combination of sex and class

```{webr-r}
titanic_df |>
  group_by(___) |>
  summarise(passengers = n(),
            survival = ___)
```

::: small
Hint: `survived` is 1 or 0, so its mean is the share who survived
:::

::: notes
group_by(sex, pclass) |> summarise(passengers = n(), survival = mean(survived)). Read the survival column together before moving on to the next slide, which gives the answer.
:::

## Class mattered as well as sex

| Survived | 1st class | 2nd class | 3rd class |
|---|---|---|---|
| Women | 97% | 89% | 49% |
| Men | 34% | 15% | 15% |

::: predict
Class mattered as well as sex. A woman in third class had about the same chance as a man in first.
:::

::: notes
Female 1st 97% (144), 2nd 89% (106), 3rd 49% (216); male 1st 34% (179), 2nd 15% (171), 3rd 15% (493). Next week we'll make charts of this ourselves with ggplot2.
Ask: what would 'children' add? mutate(status = if_else(age < 18, 'child', 'adult')) |> group_by(status) |> summarise(survival = mean(survived)): children 53%, adults 39%, and 28% for the 263 with no age. The same worked example is at the end of the Grouping chapter in the book.
:::
